title: Fintech Funding Fell 21% In Q3 As Deals Grew Scarcer

payload.text: Venture funding into fintech startups slid 21.4% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, while deal count fell nearly 31%, Crunchbase data shows, pointing to a narrower funding market with fewer rounds and continued reliance on large transactions. All told, fintech startups raised $10.6 billion globally in the third quarter of 2026, down 28.4% from $14.9 billion in Q2 2026 and 21.4% from $13.5 billion in Q3 2025. The pullback comes as investors draw sharper distinctions between companies attracting capital and those struggling to raise, according to QED Investors partner Laura Bock . “The market remains bifurcated — AI vs. not and market leaders vs. not,” she said. Forerunner founder Kirsten Green similarly described capital concentrating in fewer, larger rounds, with infrastructure, payments and stablecoin rails attracting investor interest, supported by greater regulatory clarity. Deal count drops Notably, deal count in Q3 was the lowest in the quarters covered by our analysis, dating back to the first quarter of 2018. Just 687 fintech funding rounds were recorded globally in the third quarter, compared with 789 in the previous quarter and 995 in the same period a year earlier. That represents declines of 12.9% quarter over quarter and 31% year over year. Investors are demanding stronger evidence of performance before writing checks, noted Green. For Series A and B rounds, “evidence counts for more than narrative,” she said. In emerging categories, actual usage and momentum can matter more than revenue multiples. Elsewhere, investors want efficient growth, a credible path to profitability and stronger evidence of lasting customer demand before committing to a large Series B, Green said. More startups are also combining debt and equity to limit dilution. Pullback in large rounds The quarter-over-quarter funding decline was largely driven by a pullback in large rounds. Funding from rounds of at least $100 million fell 43.3%, from $9.07 billion in Q2 to $5.15 billion in Q3, accounting for approximately 93% of the overall dollar decline. Funding from rounds below $100 million declined just 5.1% sequentially. Compared with Q3 2025, funding from rounds of at least $100 million decreased 7%, while funding from smaller rounds fell 31.4%. Large transactions remained more resilient than smaller-round funding year over year. That divide also extends to pricing. Green said a small group of companies with clear momentum command aggressive valuations, while others face greater discipline. Bock pointed to Ramp and Monzo as similarly sized businesses with widely different valuations, attributing Ramp’s premium to investor enthusiasm for its AI momentum and growth trajectory. Global mega-rounds The United States remained the largest market for fintech funding last quarter. All told, U.S. startups attracted $5.38 billion, or 50.5% of the $10.64 billion global total in Q3. The next-largest markets were Singapore with $1.28 billion (12.1%); Saudi Arabia with $626.6 million (5.9%); India with $452 million (4.2%); Brazil with $352 million (3.3%); and the United Kingdom with $337.8 million (3.2%). Singapore’s total was heavily concentrated in Ant International ’s $1.2 billion round. Despite the U.S. being the largest market for fintech funding, the quarter’s five largest funding rounds went to companies based outside the United States, ironically. Ant International, a Singapore-based provider of digital payments and financial services for businesses, raised the largest round in Q3 2026, a $1.2 billion Series A at a listed $11.2 billion post-money valuation. The data does not identify a lead investor but lists Alibaba Group and Ant Group as participants. Barq , a financial app provider based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion post-money valuation. M20 Capital , Noon Investments and Sohar International participated in the financing. Hong Kong-based Qupital , which provides financing to e-commerce businesses, secured a $300 million Series C led by M Capital at an estimated $1.36 billion post-money valuation. Jakarta, Indonesia-based Ajaib , an online investing platform, raised a $270 million Series C led by SBI Group at a $1.35 billion post-money valuation. Rounding out the top five, Riyadh-based Tabby , a digital financial services provider, raised $233 million in a Series F round led by Blue Pool Capital at a $6.5 billion post-money valuation. Late-stage fintech funding fell to $4.8 billion, down 40.4% quarter over quarter and 17.3% year over year, in Q3, per Crunchbase data. One startup lifts early-stage funding Early-stage fintech funding was comparatively resilient at $4.23 billion, up 11% quarter over quarter and down just 0.6% year over year. However, Ant International’s $1.2 billion Series A accounted for 28.4% of that total. Excluding that transaction from Q3 2026 alone, early-stage funding would have fallen 20.4% sequentially and 28.8% year over year. Early-stage deal count also dropped, from 173 in Q2 to 165 in Q3, suggesting that the increase in funding dollars did not reflect a broad expansion in activity. Fundraising expectations are rising as AI makes products faster to build and launch, Bock said. Early revenue carries less weight than sustained growth. While $1 million in annual recurring revenue once served as a common Series A benchmark, investors now want greater traction and stronger momentum, including revenue that has at least tripled over six months. “Efficiency still matters, but growth is back in focus,” she said, adding that expectations of larger potential outcomes are pushing valuations higher. Meanwhile, angel and seed funding totaled $1.12 billion, down 19.7% from Q2 and 35.2% from Q3 2025. AI reshapes investor priorities AI is primarily redirecting investment within fintech, although agents and payments are attracting some new capital, Green said. Companies without an obvious AI offering can still raise funding, but investors increasingly expect evidence that the technology improves their economics, speed or ability to reach customers. “The product has to carry that story,” she said. Bock said the distinction between companies adding AI to existing processes and those building their products around it matters. The strongest AI products deliver substantial improvements that drive rapid adoption and customers’ willingness to pay. “When investors say a company is ‘AI,’ they usually mean its growth rate is high, so growth has become the proxy,” she said. QED’s recent investments span customer support, analytics, financial advice, banking infrastructure and fraud prevention. Bock sees a durable opportunity for startups that handle the specialized integrations and accuracy requirements financial services demands — work she argues frontier AI labs are unlikely to prioritize. Green, meanwhile, said payments initiated by AI agents have moved “from ‘if’ to ‘when’” in her conversations, as major networks and processors introduced protocols to support them. She is also seeing more fintech companies seek ownership of regulated infrastructure rather than rely on outside providers. But she sees potential overfunding in stablecoin infrastructure, where many startups are pursuing the same customers, and in tools that let AI agents complete purchases for buyers, where, in her view, startup formation has outpaced transaction volume. Green sees more opportunity in the systems that make agent-driven commerce trustworthy, including fraud prevention, identity verification, agent permissions and tools that help merchants accept those purchases. “I suspect the market is treating the rails as the moat,” she said. In her view, payment infrastructure is likely to become commoditized, leaving more value with the companies that own customer relationships and earn their trust. Bock’s broader thesis is that AI could reshape financial services by sharply reducing the costs of underwriting, compliance and customer service while enabling more personalized financial products. QED is particularly interested in advice and wealth management, underwriting, insurance claims, risk and compliance, and finance back-office operations, alongside stablecoins and tokenization. “The financial services operating system will be rebuilt end-to-end,” she said. Data is as of Oct. 5, 2026. Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year. Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price.
